cr: Identifies the population as all 48,000 people who hold an annual pass from the state park agency, with N = 48,000.
Identifies the sample as the 600 randomly selected pass holders who were asked the question, with n = 600.
Explains that collecting data from every one of the 48,000 pass holders would be too difficult or time-consuming, so data were collected from a sample instead.
Identifies the datum as this pass holder's answer, yes, to the question about using an online campsite reservation system.
Describes the data set as the collection of all 600 yes-or-no answers given by the sampled pass holders.
tt: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
stem:
The state park agency sold annual park passes to 48,000 people last year. The state has about 2.1 million adult residents. The agency wants to know whether its pass holders would use a proposed online campsite reservation system. Calling every pass holder would take agency staff several months, so the agency selected a random sample of 600 pass holders and asked each one: "Would you use an online campsite reservation system? (yes or no)" All 600 pass holders in the sample answered, and 372 of them answered yes.

Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the population and the sample in this study, and give the values of N and n.

(b) Explain why the agency used a statistical study instead of collecting data from every pass holder.

(c) One pass holder in the sample answered yes. Identify the datum that this pass holder provides, and describe the data set that the agency collected.

cr: Joint relative frequency: 84/500 = 0.168.
Marginal relative frequency: 136/500 = 0.272.
Calculates the conditional relative frequency 84/240 = 0.35 for students in grades 11–12 who prefer the library.

States that there is an association, because the conditional distributions of preferred study location differ between the grade groups, citing at least one comparison of conditional relative frequencies (for example 0.20 versus 0.35 for the library, or 0.60 versus 0.40 for home).
Computes 84/136 ≈ 0.618, the proportion of library-preferring students who are in grades 11–12.
Concludes that the data support the claim because 0.618 is greater than 0.5 (more than half of library-preferring students are in grades 11–12).
tt: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables
stem:
A high school surveyed 500 of its students about where they prefer to study. Each student was classified by grade group and by preferred study location. The results are shown in the table.

Grade group | Home | Library | Café | Total
Grades 9–10 | 156 | 52 | 52 | 260
Grades 11–12 | 96 | 84 | 60 | 240
Total | 252 | 136 | 112 | 500

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) For these 500 students, calculate the joint relative frequency of being in grades 11–12 and preferring the library, and calculate the marginal relative frequency of preferring the library.

(b) In grades 9–10, 52 of the 260 students (0.20) prefer the library. Calculate the proportion of students in grades 11–12 who prefer the library. Based on the conditional relative frequencies of preferred study location for the two grade groups, is there an association between grade group and preferred study location for these students? Justify your answer.

(c) A student claims: "Most of the students who prefer the library are in grades 11–12." Use an appropriate relative frequency to determine whether the data support this claim.

cr: Computes a pair of probabilities that would be equal if the events were independent, such as P(A | M) = 120/360 ≈ 0.333 and P(A) = 240/800 = 0.30, or P(A ∩ M) = 0.15 and P(A)·P(M) = 0.30 × 0.45 = 0.135.
Concludes that A and M are not independent because the compared probabilities are not equal (0.333 ≠ 0.30, or 0.15 ≠ 0.135).
P(pastry and app) = 0.35 × 0.50 = 0.175.
tt: Independent Events and Unions of Events
stem:
A coffee shop recorded 800 transactions during one week. Each transaction was classified by whether the customer ordered a pastry and whether the customer paid with the shop's mobile app.

Order | Paid with app | Did not pay with app | Total
Ordered a pastry | 120 | 120 | 240
No pastry | 240 | 320 | 560
Total | 360 | 440 | 800

One of these 800 transactions is selected at random. Let A be the event that the customer ordered a pastry, and let M be the event that the customer paid with the mobile app.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find P(A ∪ M), the probability that the selected customer ordered a pastry or paid with the app (or both). Show your work.

(b) Are events A and M independent? Justify your answer using probabilities.

(c) At a new location, the manager models ordering a pastry and paying with the app as independent events, with probability 0.35 that a customer orders a pastry and probability 0.50 that a customer pays with the app. Under this model, find the probability that a randomly selected customer orders a pastry and pays with the app, and the probability that the customer orders a pastry or pays with the app (or both).

cr: Identifies Estimator A as appearing unbiased because the mean of its simulated values, 0.401, is approximately equal to the true proportion, 0.40.
Identifies Estimator B as biased because the mean of its simulated values, 0.429, is greater than 0.40, so on average B overestimates the true proportion.
Calculates Estimator A = 7/10 = 0.70.
Calculates Estimator B = (7 + 2)/14 = 9/14 ≈ 0.643.
Identifies 0.70, the value of Estimator A (the sample proportion), as the unbiased point estimate to report.

Explains that unbiased describes the average of the estimator's values over many random samples, so in a particular sample the value of Estimator A can be farther from the true proportion than the value of Estimator B.
tt: Estimators
stem:
A seed company wants to estimate p, the proportion of all seeds in a large bin that germinate. Two estimators are proposed, each based on a random sample of 10 seeds, where X is the number of sampled seeds that germinate.

Estimator A: X/10 (the sample proportion)
Estimator B: (X + 2)/14

To study the estimators, a statistics class used a computer to simulate 1,000 random samples of 10 seeds from a large bin in which exactly 40% of the seeds germinate. For each simulated sample, the class calculated the value of both estimators. The results are summarized in the table.

Estimator | Mean of the 1,000 simulated values
A | 0.401
B | 0.429

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Based on the simulation, which estimator appears to be unbiased and which appears to be biased? Justify your answers.

(b) The company then selects a random sample of 10 seeds from a new bin whose germination proportion is unknown, and 7 of the 10 seeds germinate. Calculate the value of each estimator for this sample, and identify which value the company should report as an unbiased point estimate of the proportion of all seeds in the new bin that germinate.

(c) A student says, "Because Estimator A is unbiased, its value from any single sample will be closer to the true proportion than the value of Estimator B." Explain why the student's statement is incorrect.

cr: Names a two-sample z-interval for a difference between two population proportions.
Defines the parameter as p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all trees in the northern section with beetle damage and p₂ is the proportion of all trees in the southern section with beetle damage.
States that each sample is at most 10% of its section: 200 and 250 are both less than 0.10(50,000) = 5,000.
States that the numbers of observed successes and failures, 46, 154, 35 and 215, are all at least 10.
95% confidence interval: 0.09 ± 1.96(0.0370) ≈ 0.09 ± 0.0725, giving about (0.018, 0.162) for northern minus southern.
tt: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
stem:
A forestry agency wants to estimate the difference between the proportions of trees with beetle damage in the northern and southern sections of a large state forest. Each section contains more than 50,000 trees. The agency selected a random sample of 200 trees from the northern section and, independently, a random sample of 250 trees from the southern section. Of the 200 northern trees, 46 had beetle damage; of the 250 southern trees, 35 had beetle damage.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the appropriate confidence interval procedure, and define the parameter of interest in context.

(b) The two samples were selected randomly and independently. Verify the 10% condition and the normality condition for this procedure.

(c) Calculate the standard error of the difference in sample proportions and a 95% confidence interval for the parameter you defined. Show your work.

cr: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.046 to 0.174 captures the difference (Riverton minus Lakeside) between the proportions of all adult residents of each town who used a public library in the past month.

Explains that if many pairs of independent random samples of 500 Riverton adults and 400 Lakeside adults were taken and a 95% interval calculated from each pair, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true difference p₁ − p₂ in the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month.
States that the interval supports the first claim (gives convincing evidence of a difference) because 0 is not in the interval; every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is positive.
States that the interval does not support the second claim because every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is less than 0.20 (0.20 is above the upper limit 0.174).
Explains that the interval is calculated from random samples, so it may or may not contain the true difference; the 95% confidence level means about 5% of such intervals miss the true difference.
tt: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
stem:
A regional library board selected a random sample of 500 adult residents of Riverton and, independently, a random sample of 400 adult residents of Lakeside. Each town has more than 20,000 adult residents. In the samples, 230 of the Riverton residents (0.46) and 140 of the Lakeside residents (0.35) said they had used a public library in the past month. All conditions for inference were met, and the board calculated a 95% confidence interval for p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all adult residents of Riverton who used a public library in the past month and p₂ is the proportion of all adult residents of Lakeside who used a public library in the past month. The interval is (0.046, 0.174).

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

(b) Interpret the 95% confidence level in context.

(c) One board member claims that the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month are different in the two towns. A second board member claims that Riverton's proportion is more than 20 percentage points higher than Lakeside's. Does the interval support each claim? Explain.

(d) A resident says, "Since the interval was calculated from the data, the true difference p₁ − p₂ must be between 0.046 and 0.174." Explain why the resident's statement is not correct.

cr: Names a two-sample z-test for a difference between two population proportions.

Defines p₁ as the true proportion of people like these volunteers who would report falling asleep faster after two weeks of the bedtime breathing exercise, and p₂ as the true proportion who would report falling asleep faster after two weeks of bedtime reading.
H₀: p₁ = p₂ (or p₁ − p₂ = 0) and Hₐ: p₁ > p₂ (or p₁ − p₂ > 0), with p₁ for the breathing exercise and p₂ for reading.
States that the randomization condition is met because the volunteers were randomly assigned to the two treatments.
Explains that the 10% condition is not needed because the data come from a randomized experiment (the volunteers were randomly assigned to the two treatments).
Computes the combined proportion p̂c = (52 + 38)/(90 + 90) = 0.50 and states that n₁p̂c = 45, n₁(1 − p̂c) = 45, n₂p̂c = 45 and n₂(1 − p̂c) = 45 are all at least 10.
tt: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
stem:
A researcher recruited 180 adult volunteers who reported trouble falling asleep. The volunteers were randomly assigned to two groups of 90. Each night for two weeks, one group did a 10-minute breathing exercise at bedtime and the other group read a printed book for 10 minutes at bedtime. At the end of the two weeks, 52 of the 90 volunteers in the breathing group and 38 of the 90 volunteers in the reading group reported that they fell asleep faster. The researcher wants to know whether the data provide convincing evidence that the breathing exercise is more effective than reading at helping people like these volunteers fall asleep faster.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the appropriate testing procedure, and define the parameters of interest in context.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the researcher's test.

(c) Verify the conditions for this test. In your answer, explain why the 10% condition does not need to be checked.

cr: p-value = 2P(Z ≥ 2.18) ≈ 0.029, using both tails because the alternative hypothesis is two-sided.

States that, assuming the proportions of all households that compost food waste are the same in the two towns, the probability of getting a difference in sample proportions of 0.08 or more in either direction (|p̂₁ − p̂₂| ≥ 0.08) is about 0.029.

Because the p-value ≈ 0.029 is less than α = 0.05, the group rejects H₀; there is convincing statistical evidence that the proportion of all Town A households that compost food waste is different from the proportion of all Town B households that compost food waste.
tt: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
stem:
An environmental group wants to know whether the proportion of households that compost food waste differs between two large towns, Town A (about 30,000 households) and Town B (about 22,000 households). The group selected a random sample of 300 households in Town A and, independently, a random sample of 250 households in Town B. In the samples, 84 of the Town A households and 50 of the Town B households compost food waste.

Let p₁ be the proportion of all Town A households that compost food waste, and let p₂ be the proportion of all Town B households that compost food waste. The group tests H₀: p₁ = p₂ versus Hₐ: p₁ ≠ p₂ at the α = 0.05 significance level. All conditions for inference are met.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Calculate the combined (pooled) sample proportion and the test statistic. Show your work.

(b) Find the p-value of the test.

(c) Interpret the p-value in context.

(d) What conclusion should the group make at the α = 0.05 significance level? Justify your answer.

cr: Identifies a chi-square test for homogeneity, because the researcher took separate (independent) random samples from three populations (the adults of the three cities) and compares the distribution of one categorical variable, main news source, across those populations.

H₀: The distribution of main news source (television, online, other) is the same for adults in all three cities. Hₐ: The distribution of main news source is not the same for adults in all three cities (it differs for at least one city).
States that each sample of 150 is at most 10% of its city's adults: 150 ≤ 0.10(500,000) = 50,000.
States that all expected counts are greater than 5 (the smallest is 19.3).
States that the chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom is skewed right, and that the distribution with 10 degrees of freedom is less skewed (its skew is less pronounced).

Explains that the chi-square statistic measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to the expected counts, so a large value indicates that the observed counts are far from the counts expected if the distributions were the same.
tt: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
stem:
A media researcher wants to know whether the distribution of adults' main news source differs among three large cities. The researcher selected independent random samples of 150 adults from each city (each city has more than 500,000 adults) and recorded each adult's main news source. The observed counts are shown in the table, with the expected counts (calculated assuming the distribution of main news source is the same in the three cities) in parentheses.

City | Television | Online | Other | Total
City A | 60 (53.0) | 70 (77.7) | 20 (19.3) | 150
City B | 45 (53.0) | 85 (77.7) | 20 (19.3) | 150
City C | 54 (53.0) | 78 (77.7) | 18 (19.3) | 150
Total | 159 | 233 | 58 | 450

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the appropriate chi-square test, and explain why it is appropriate for this study.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses in context.

(c) The samples were independent random samples. Verify the 10% condition and the expected counts condition for the test.

(d) If the null hypothesis is true, the test statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Describe the shape of this distribution and how it compares with the shape of a chi-square distribution with 10 degrees of freedom. Then explain what a large value of the chi-square statistic would indicate about the observed counts compared with the expected counts.

cr: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.511 to 0.609 captures the proportion of all registered voters in the state who support the ballot measure.

Explains that if many random samples of 400 registered voters were taken from this state and a 95% confidence interval were calculated from each, about 95% of those intervals would capture the proportion of all the state's registered voters who support the measure.
States that the interval supports the majority claim (provides convincing evidence for it) because every value in the interval from 0.511 to 0.609 is greater than 0.50.
States that the interval does not support the 65% claim because 0.65 is not in the interval; every plausible value is less than 0.65.
States that the margin of error would be larger because a 99% confidence level uses a larger critical value (z* ≈ 2.576 instead of 1.96).
States that the width would be about half as large (about 0.049 instead of 0.098), because the width is approximately proportional to 1/√n and √(1,600/400) = 2.
tt: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
stem:
A polling organization selected a random sample of 400 registered voters from a state with about 6 million registered voters. Of the voters sampled, 224 said they support a proposed ballot measure. All conditions for inference were met, and the organization reported a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all the state's registered voters who support the measure: (0.511, 0.609).

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

(b) Interpret the 95% confidence level in context.

(c) Supporters of the measure claim that a majority of the state's registered voters support it. The measure's sponsor claims that 65% of the state's registered voters support it. Does the interval support each claim? Explain.

(d) Answer each question about how the interval would change. First, if the organization had used a 99% confidence level with the same sample, would the margin of error be larger, smaller, or the same? Explain. Second, if the organization had instead used a random sample of 1,600 registered voters and obtained the same sample proportion, about how would the width of the 95% confidence interval compare with the width of (0.511, 0.609)? Explain.

cr: Names a one-sample z-test for a population proportion.
Defines p as the proportion of all the city's streetlights that are out of service (after the repair program).
H₀: p = 0.10 (or H₀: p ≥ 0.10, tested at 0.10) and Hₐ: p < 0.10.
States that the randomization condition is met because the inspector checked a random sample of the city's streetlights.
States that the 10% condition is met because 120 ≤ 0.10(9,400) = 940 (equivalently, 9,400 ≥ 10 × 120 = 1,200).
States that the classmate is not correct because the test's normality condition uses the null value p₀ = 0.10: np₀ = 120(0.10) = 12 and n(1 − p₀) = 120(0.90) = 108 are both at least 10.
tt: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion
stem:
A city reports that 10% of its 9,400 streetlights are out of service. After a new repair program, the city's public works department believes that the proportion of the city's streetlights that are out of service has decreased. An inspector checks a random sample of 120 of the city's streetlights and finds that 9 of them are out of service. The department plans to use these data to test its belief.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the appropriate testing procedure, and define the parameter of interest in context.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the department's test.

(c) Verify the randomization condition and the 10% condition for this test.

(d) A classmate says that the normality condition for this test is not met because only 9 of the sampled streetlights were out of service. Is the classmate correct? Explain.

cr: Estimates the p-value as 4/200 = 0.02 by counting the simulated samples with 20 or more riders who paid with the app (2 + 2 = 4).
Describes the p-value as the probability of getting 20 or more riders who pay with the app in a random sample of 50 riders (a result as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed).
States that this probability is calculated assuming that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is 0.25.

Explains that because the p-value (about 0.02) is small, getting 20 or more app users in a sample of 50 would be unusual if p were 0.25, so the data provide evidence that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.25.

Explains that a p-value that is not small means the observed result would not be unusual if p were 0.25, so it fails to provide convincing evidence for Hₐ, but it does not provide evidence that H₀ is true or prove that p = 0.25.
tt: p-Values
stem:
A city transit agency reports that 25% of its riders pay their fares with a mobile app. A transportation analyst believes the proportion is greater than 25%. In a random sample of 50 of the agency's riders, 20 paid with the mobile app. The analyst will test H₀: p = 0.25 versus Hₐ: p > 0.25, where p is the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the mobile app.

To obtain the null distribution, the analyst used a computer to simulate 200 random samples of 50 riders, assuming p = 0.25, and recorded the number of riders in each simulated sample who paid with the app. The results are shown in the table.

Number who paid with app | Number of simulated samples
6 or fewer | 4
7 | 6
8 | 11
9 | 17
10 | 22
11 | 25
12 | 26
13 | 24
14 | 20
15 | 15
16 | 11
17 | 7
18 | 5
19 | 3
20 | 2
21 or more | 2
Total | 200

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Use the simulation results to estimate the p-value of the test. Show how you obtained it.

(b) Interpret the p-value you estimated in context.

(c) What does the p-value suggest about the agency's report that 25% of its riders pay with the app? Explain.

(d) A second analyst took a different random sample of 50 riders and obtained a p-value of 0.41 for the same test. The second analyst concluded that this proves that exactly 25% of all the agency's riders pay with the app. Explain why this conclusion is not justified.

cr: Type I error: the chain finds convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised and rejects the shipment, when in fact the proportion of bruised apples in the shipment is 0.05 (not greater than 0.05).
Type II error: the chain does not find convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples are bruised and accepts the shipment, when in fact more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised.
Chooses α = 0.10 because a larger significance level makes it easier to reject H₀, which increases the power and decreases the probability of a Type II error.
Calculates the probability of a Type II error as 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.
States that the probability of a Type II error would decrease (the power would increase) because a larger sample size decreases the standard error.
tt: Potential Errors When Performing Tests
stem:
A grocery chain buys apples in shipments of 20,000 apples. Before accepting a shipment, the chain inspects a random sample of 400 apples from it. The chain will reject the shipment if the sample gives convincing evidence that more than 5% of the apples in the shipment are bruised. For each shipment, the chain tests H₀: p = 0.05 versus Hₐ: p > 0.05, where p is the proportion of all apples in the shipment that are bruised.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in context.

(b) The chain considers a Type II error more serious than a Type I error because bruised apples lead to customer complaints. Should the chain use a significance level of α = 0.01 or α = 0.10? Explain.

(c) With α = 0.05 and a sample of 400 apples, the power of the test is about 0.81 when 8% of the apples in a shipment are bruised. Find the probability of a Type II error for such a shipment. Then, if the chain increased its sample size to 800 apples (keeping α = 0.05), would the probability of a Type II error for such a shipment increase, decrease, or stay the same? Explain.

cr: States that each sample is at most 10% of its population: 120 ≤ 0.10(18,000) = 1,800 and 100 ≤ 0.10(25,000) = 2,500.
States that n₁p₁ = 74.4, n₁(1 − p₁) = 45.6, n₂p₂ = 48 and n₂(1 − p₂) = 52 are all at least 10, so the sampling distribution is approximately normal.
Identifies the event as p̂₁ − p̂₂ < 0 and uses a normal model with mean 0.14 and standard deviation 0.0668, for example z = (0 − 0.14)/0.0668 ≈ −2.10.
Finds the probability ≈ 0.018.
tt: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions
stem:
At University X, which has 18,000 students, 62% of the students live on campus. At University Y, which has 25,000 students, 48% of the students live on campus. A researcher will select a random sample of 120 students from University X and, independently, a random sample of 100 students from University Y. Let p̂₁ be the proportion of the sampled University X students who live on campus, and let p̂₂ be the proportion of the sampled University Y students who live on campus.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the mean and the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂.

(b) The two samples will be independent random samples. Verify the remaining conditions that justify using this standard deviation formula and modeling the sampling distribution of p̂₁ − p̂₂ as approximately normal.

(c) Find the probability that the proportion of sampled University X students who live on campus is less than the proportion of sampled University Y students who live on campus. Show your work.

cr: States that the trout were randomly selected, which meets the random condition.
States that the 10% condition is met because the lake holds more than 10 × 22 = 220 trout.
States that although n = 22 is less than 30, the sample is roughly symmetric with no outliers, so the sample data condition is met.
Sets up the interval as 31.4 ± 2.080(4.2/√22), with the sample mean, t*, s and n correctly substituted (the standard error is about 0.895 cm).
Gives the interval 31.4 ± 1.86, or (29.54, 33.26) cm.
States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 29.54 to 33.26 cm captures the true mean length of all rainbow trout in the lake.

stem:
A fisheries biologist wants to estimate the mean length of rainbow trout in a large lake that holds many thousands of trout. She catches and measures a random sample of 22 trout. The sample mean length is 31.4 cm and the sample standard deviation is 4.2 cm. A dotplot of the 22 lengths is roughly symmetric, with no outliers.

For 95% confidence with 21 degrees of freedom, the critical value is t* = 2.080.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Check the conditions for constructing a t interval for the population mean length.

(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean length of all rainbow trout in the lake.

(c) Interpret the interval in the context of the study.

cr: Explains that each student provides both a before score and an after score, so the two sets of scores are paired (not independent), and analyzing the differences accounts for the pairing.
Defines μd as the true mean difference (score after − score before) in quiz scores for all students at the school.
Computes the interval 3.9 ± 1.771(5.1/√14), which is approximately (1.49, 6.31) points.
States that we are 90% confident that the interval from 1.49 to 6.31 points captures the true mean change (after − before) in quiz scores for all students at the school.
Interprets the confidence level: if the teacher repeated the sampling process many times, about 90% of the intervals constructed this way would capture the true mean difference.
tt: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference
stem:
A teacher wants to estimate the mean change in quiz scores when students use a review app. She randomly selects 14 of the 1,150 students at her school. Each student takes a quiz on a topic, studies the topic with the app for a week, and then takes a different quiz of equal difficulty on the same topic. For each student she computes the difference d = (score after) − (score before).

The 14 differences have a mean of 3.9 points and a standard deviation of 5.1 points. Their distribution has no strong skewness and no outliers.

For 90% confidence with 13 degrees of freedom, the critical value is t* = 1.771.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

stem:
A city's emergency services department states that the mean response time for ambulance calls is 8.0 minutes. A resident believes the true mean response time is longer. The resident obtains the department's records of about 5,400 calls from the past year and takes a simple random sample of 36 of those calls. The sample mean response time is 8.7 minutes and the sample standard deviation is 2.9 minutes. The distribution of the 36 response times is skewed to the right, with no extreme outliers.

Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses for a test of the resident's belief, defining any parameter you use.

(b) Name the inference procedure that is appropriate for these hypotheses.

(c) The calls are a simple random sample. Verify the 10% condition and the sample data condition for using this procedure.

States Ha: μd > 0 seconds.

tt: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Population Mean Difference
stem:
A sports scientist wants to know whether chewing caffeine gum before a 5 km run reduces the mean running time. She recruits 15 volunteer runners. Each runner completes two 5 km time trials one week apart, once after chewing caffeine gum and once after chewing placebo gum. For each runner, the order of the two conditions is assigned at random.

For each runner she records d = (time after placebo gum) − (time after caffeine gum), in seconds, so a positive d means the runner was faster with caffeine. The 15 values of d have a mean of 14 seconds and a standard deviation of 21 seconds. The distribution of the 15 values of d is roughly symmetric, with no outliers.

Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Explain why a matched-pairs procedure is appropriate here instead of a two-sample procedure.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses for the scientist's test, defining any parameter you use.

(c) Verify the conditions for using a matched-pairs t procedure.

tt: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means
stem:
Two machines fill bags of rice. Machine 1 fills bags with a mean weight of μ1 = 502 g and a standard deviation of σ1 = 6 g. Machine 2 fills bags with a mean weight of μ2 = 500 g and a standard deviation of σ2 = 5 g. The shapes of the two distributions of bag weights are not known.

An inspector takes an independent random sample of n1 = 36 bags from Machine 1 and an independent random sample of n2 = 30 bags from Machine 2, and computes the difference in the sample means, x̄1 − x̄2. Each machine fills at least 5,000 bags in a day.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) What is the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2?

(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2.

(c) Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and justify your answer.

(d) Suppose the inspector increases the sample from Machine 2 to 60 bags and keeps 36 bags from Machine 1. Calculate the new standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and state whether it is smaller than, larger than, or the same as before.

tt: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means
stem:
A consumer lab compares two brands of rechargeable flashlight batteries. The battery life of Brand A is normally distributed with a mean of 18.0 hours and a standard deviation of 2.4 hours. The battery life of Brand B is normally distributed with a mean of 16.5 hours and a standard deviation of 3.0 hours.

The lab tests an independent random sample of 9 Brand A batteries and an independent random sample of 12 Brand B batteries, and computes the difference in the sample means, x̄A − x̄B.

A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Find the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B.

(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B.

(c) Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B, and justify your answer even though both sample sizes are less than 30.

(d) A second lab tests the same sample sizes of 9 and 12 batteries but does not know the shape of either population. Can it assume that the sampling distribution of x̄A − x̄B is approximately normal? Explain.
